chapters.title: Chapter 5: Central Banks in Crisis, and What Investors Learn

lessons.title: The 2008 Global Financial Crisis: Central Banks as Lenders of Last Resort

body.text: In September 2008, the world discovered what happens when trust between banks disappears overnight. Central banks stopped the collapse by doing the one thing only they can do: lending without limit when no one else would. The crisis turned lender of last resort from a textbook phrase into the defining job of every modern central bank, and India learned it was far less insulated than it believed.

children.text: Chapter 5 turns to crises, where central banks are tested hardest and investors learn the most. We start with the one that reshaped everything that followed: the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. You studied the lender of last resort idea in Chapter 1. Here you will see it in action on a global scale, and how the RBI used almost every tool in this course to protect India.
How the Crisis Built Up

markDefs.definition: Home loans given to borrowers with poor credit histories, often with low initial rates that reset higher later. Their mass default triggered the 2008 crisis.

children.text: Through the mid-2000s, US banks and lenders gave home loans to borrowers with weak credit, known as
subprime mortgages

. These loans were bundled into complex securities, rated as safe, and sold to banks and investors worldwide. When US house prices started falling in 2006 and 2007, defaults surged, and nobody knew which institutions held the toxic assets.

markDefs.definition: A situation where solvent or near-solvent institutions cannot get short-term funding because lenders refuse to lend, forcing fire sales of assets or failure.

children.text: Banks stopped trusting each other. Short-term lending between banks, the plumbing of the financial system, froze. Institutions that relied on borrowing overnight to fund long-term assets suddenly could not roll over their debts. This was a
liquidity crisis
that threatened to become a solvency crisis for the whole system.
The Fall of 2008

body.title: From Bear Stearns to Zero Rates

events.title: Bear Stearns rescued
events.description: JPMorgan Chase agrees to buy the collapsing investment bank. The New York Fed backs the deal by funding $29 billion of Bear Stearns' less liquid assets.

events.title: Lehman Brothers fails
events.description: With $639 billion in assets and $613 billion in debts, it becomes the largest bankruptcy in US history. The Fed and US Treasury choose not to rescue it.

events.title: AIG bailed out
events.description: The Fed agrees to lend up to $85 billion to insurer AIG, taking a 79.9% equity stake, because its failure could topple banks worldwide.

events.title: TARP becomes law
events.description: The US Congress authorises the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program to stabilise banks.

events.title: Swap lines peak
events.description: The Fed's dollar swap lines with other central banks reach $583 billion, about a quarter of its assets, so banks worldwide can get dollars.

events.title: Rates cut to near zero
events.description: The Fed cuts the federal funds rate to 0% to 0.25%, and soon launches QE, as you saw in Chapter 4.

body.text: Letting Lehman fail was meant to show that reckless firms would not always be rescued. Instead, it triggered panic, because investors suddenly feared any institution could collapse. The very next day the Fed rescued AIG. The lesson central banks took away: in a systemic panic, allowing one major failure can be far costlier than stepping in.

children.text: The Lender of Last Resort, Rewritten

markDefs.definition: The principle, from Walter Bagehot's 1873 book Lombard Street, that in a financial panic a central bank should lend freely to solvent institutions against good collateral at a penalty rate.

children.text: The classic rule for a lender of last resort comes from Walter Bagehot, a 19th-century British writer: in a panic, lend freely, against good collateral, at a high rate. It is often called
Bagehot's dictum
. In 2008, central banks stretched it further than ever before.

columns.label: Classic lender of last resort
points: Lend short-term at a penalty rate

columns.label: What central banks actually did in 2008
points: Lent to investment banks and an insurer, AIG
Accepted a wide range of riskier assets
Cut rates to near zero and bought assets through QE
Supplied dollars across borders through swap lines

body.title: Why Rescue AIG After Letting Lehman Fail?
body.question: The Fed let Lehman Brothers fail on 15 September 2008 but lent up to $85 billion to AIG the next day. What best explains the different treatment?
options: AIG was a bank and Lehman was not
AIG had sold insurance-like protection to banks worldwide, so its collapse threatened to spread losses across the entire financial system
The Fed is legally barred from lending to investment banks
body.explanation: AIG had written huge amounts of credit protection that banks around the world relied on. If it failed, those banks would suddenly face losses too, turning one failure into many. Lehman's collapse had already shown how badly panic could spread, so the Fed stepped in to stop a chain reaction. The deciding question was systemic risk, not the type of company.

children.text: Why India Was Hit, Despite Having No Subprime Mess
Indian banks held very little of the toxic US mortgage securities, and many policymakers initially believed India was decoupled from the crisis. It was not. The shock arrived through three channels.

cells: Foreign investors fled
FIIs pulled a net ₹52,987 crore out of Indian shares in 2008, then a record, as global funds rushed to raise cash and cut risk.
Dollars dried up
Indian companies that relied on foreign loans and trade credit found overseas funding frozen, so they turned to Indian banks and markets for rupees instead.
Confidence cracked
Rumours spread about Indian banks, and exports slowed as the global economy slumped.

stats.label: Sensex, 9 March 2009
stats.context: Near the bottom of the crash

stats.label: Rupee, end-March 2009
stats.context: After touching a record 52.18 in March 2009

body.title: How Far Did the Sensex Fall?
body.prompt: The Sensex closed at a high of 20,873 on 8 January 2008 and was at 8,160 on 9 March 2009. What was the percentage fall? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (8,160 − 20,873) ÷ 20,873 × 100 = -60.9%. The Sensex lost more than 60% of its value in about 14 months. An investor who had put ₹1,00,000 in at the January 2008 peak would have seen it shrink to under ₹40,000 at the trough, before the market recovered.

body.title: What Happened to the Rupee?
body.prompt: The rupee was 40.12 per dollar at the end of March 2008 and 50.75 at the end of March 2009. By what percentage did the dollar's price in rupees rise? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (50.75 − 40.12) ÷ 40.12 × 100 = 26.5%. Every dollar cost about a quarter more in rupees within a year. For importers and companies with dollar loans, that was a severe shock on top of the stock market crash.

children.text: The ICICI Bank Scare

On 30 September 2008, just two weeks after Lehman, rumours spread that ICICI Bank, then India's largest private sector bank, was in trouble because of exposure to the crisis. Crowds formed at some branches and ATMs as customers withdrew cash. The bank called the rumours baseless. Then the RBI did something unusual: it publicly stated that ICICI Bank had enough liquidity and that the RBI had arranged to provide adequate cash to meet customer demand. The run faded.

body.text: This was the lender of last resort principle in its purest form, applied in India. The RBI did not need to lend very much. Its credible public promise to supply cash was enough to stop depositors panicking. Confidence, as you learned in Chapter 1, is what a central bank ultimately protects.

children.text: How the RBI Fought Back
From October 2008, under newly appointed Governor D. Subbarao, the RBI used almost every tool you studied in Chapter 2, often in quick succession.

cells: Repo rate
Cut from a peak of 9% to 4.75% by April 2009, a total of 425 basis points
To slash borrowing costs and support growth
CRR
Cut by 400 basis points, from 9% to 5%, releasing about ₹1.6 lakh crore
To put cash directly into banks as funding markets froze
Special liquidity windows
Extra funding lines so banks could support mutual funds and NBFCs hit by redemptions
To stop panic in non-bank lenders and funds from spreading
Forex reserves
Sold dollars to smooth the rupee's fall
To prevent a disorderly currency collapse
Public reassurance
Statements backing banks such as ICICI Bank
To stop rumour-driven bank runs

children.text: By early 2009, the RBI estimated that the combined liquidity impact of its measures since October 2008 was over ₹3.88 lakh crore. Meanwhile, reserves did the heavy lifting on the currency front.

body.title: How Much Firepower Was Used?
body.prompt: India's forex reserves hit a record $316.17 billion in May 2008 and were about $252 billion at the end of March 2009. What was the percentage fall? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ($252 billion − $316.17 billion) ÷ $316.17 billion × 100 = -20.3%. About a fifth of the reserves were gone within a year, through dollar sales and valuation changes. The episode is a big reason the RBI later built reserves far higher, reaching a record $785.71 billion in September 2026.

children.text: The Outcome

India's economy slowed but did not collapse. GDP growth fell to about 6.7% in 2008-09, down from around 9% in the three years before. Markets rebounded sharply in 2009 as global central banks flooded the system with liquidity. Globally, the crisis left a long legacy: near-zero interest rates for years, QE, much stricter bank capital rules, and a public backlash against bank bailouts.

body.title: Go Deeper: Why Banks Were So Fragile

children.text: Before 2008, many global banks and investment banks funded long-term, hard-to-sell assets with very short-term borrowing, often overnight. They also carried very high leverage: small amounts of capital supporting huge balance sheets. Lehman Brothers, for example, had $639 billion of assets against $613 billion of debts, leaving only about $26 billion of cushion.

When lenders refused to roll over overnight funding, these firms had to sell assets at fire-sale prices, which pushed prices down further and forced others to sell too. After the crisis, global regulators introduced the Basel III rules, requiring banks to hold more capital and more liquid assets, including the Liquidity Coverage Ratio you met in Chapter 2.

body.title: Your Portfolio in October 2008
body.scenario: It is mid-October 2008. You have ₹5 lakh in Indian equity mutual funds, down about 50% from your purchase price in January. The news is full of bank failures, the Sensex has crashed to around 10,000, and a colleague says the entire financial system is about to collapse. You also have ₹2 lakh in a fixed deposit with a large private bank.
body.prompt: What would you do with your equity funds and your fixed deposit, and what signals from central banks would you watch?
body.modelAnswer: Selling equity funds after a 50% fall locks in the loss permanently. The key question is whether the financial system itself survives, and here central bank actions matter most. Watch for exactly what happened: the Fed and other central banks lending without limit and cutting rates, governments recapitalising banks, and the RBI cutting the repo rate and CRR aggressively. When central banks act on that scale, a total system collapse becomes much less likely, even if markets fall further first. The Sensex did fall further, to around 8,160 by March 2009, but then more than doubled within about a year. For the fixed deposit, the RBI's public backing of ICICI Bank showed that it would not let a major Indian bank fail, and deposit insurance also covered part of the amount. Panic withdrawals would not have made you safer. The durable lesson: during a systemic crisis, watch what central banks do, avoid forced selling, and keep enough cash so you never have to sell at the bottom.

body.title: Learn From 2008
steps: Look up the Sensex chart from January 2008 to December 2010 and note how long it took to regain its 2008 peak
Compare India's forex reserves in March 2009 with the latest figure, and think about how that changes India's crisis readiness
Find the current CRR and repo rate, and note how much room the RBI has to cut if a crisis hit today
Check whether you hold an emergency fund large enough to avoid selling investments in a market crash
Read the RBI's latest Financial Stability Report summary for current risks to Indian banks

points: The 2008 crisis began with US subprime mortgages, but became a global liquidity crisis when banks stopped trusting and lending to each other.
After Lehman Brothers failed on 15 September 2008, central banks acted as lenders of last resort on an unprecedented scale: rescuing AIG, cutting rates to zero and opening swap lines.
India had little subprime exposure but was hit through FII outflows of ₹52,987 crore, frozen dollar funding and shaken confidence.
The Sensex fell over 60% from its January 2008 peak by March 2009, and the rupee weakened from about 40 to 51 per dollar.
The RBI cut the repo rate by 425 basis points to 4.75% and CRR by 400 basis points, and publicly backed ICICI Bank to stop a run.
The crisis taught India to build far larger forex reserves and taught regulators worldwide to demand stronger bank capital and liquidity.
